title: Quiz: The Shewhart Cycle — PDCA and PDSA

questions.text: What is the primary philosophical difference between the Check phase in PDCA and the Study phase in PDSA?
options: Check involves collecting more data; Study only reviews existing data
Check verifies whether targets were met; Study analyses why results occurred and generates knowledge
Check is used in manufacturing; Study is restricted to healthcare improvement
Check and Study are identical — the terms are used interchangeably by Deming
questions.explanation: Deming revised PDCA to PDSA because 'Check' implies passive inspection — confirming whether a goal was hit. 'Study' demands deeper scientific analysis: understanding the mechanism behind the result so that the knowledge generated can seed the next cycle and prevent recurrence.

questions.text: In the PDCA cycle, the Act phase should be performed when:
options: Targets are partially met — Act means adjusting the target downward
The change is confirmed effective — standardise and deploy at full scale; or if ineffective, use new learning to plan the next cycle
Management approves the plan document during the planning phase
The Do phase is complete regardless of whether the results are positive
questions.explanation: Act has two branches: (1) if the change worked, standardise it and implement fully; (2) if it did not work, abandon or modify it and use the learning from Study to design a better Plan for the next cycle. Act is never unconditional deployment.

questions.text: A hospital runs four PDCA cycles and achieves wait-time reductions of −10 min, −6 min, −3 min, and −1 min. This pattern of decreasing returns per cycle most likely reflects:
options: Poor execution of later cycles due to staff fatigue
The natural exhaustion of easy-to-fix causes; subsequent cycles address deeper, harder-to-resolve issues
A fundamental flaw in the PDCA model that makes it unsuitable for healthcare
Regression to the mean — the early gains were due to random variation
questions.explanation: Diminishing returns per cycle are normal and expected in continuous improvement. Early cycles capture low-hanging fruit (high-impact, easily fixed causes). Later cycles address structural or systemic causes requiring more effort for smaller incremental gains. This is not a failure of PDCA; it is the programme working correctly.

questions.text: Which of the following quality frameworks is best described as a detailed, structured elaboration of the Plan and Do phases of PDCA?
questions.explanation: Six Sigma DMAIC (Define-Measure-Analyse-Improve-Control) is essentially an expanded, statistically rigorous version of the Plan and Do phases, with Define/Measure/Analyse mapping to Plan, Improve to Do, and Control to Check/Act. DMAIC is PDCA with explicit statistical tools at every step.

questions.text: The recommended practice in PDCA is to test a change at full deployment scale immediately in the Do phase to obtain representative results.
questions.explanation: The Do phase should test changes on a small, controlled scale (one machine, one shift, one ward) before full deployment. Small-scale tests limit the risk of a failed change causing widespread disruption, generate faster learning cycles, and allow refinement before commitment. Full-scale rollout comes only after the Act phase confirms the change is effective.
